intro.title: Discover Venice Canal Historic District
intro.description:
Venice Canal Historic District is a historic canal neighborhood in the Venice area of Los Angeles, California. It was created in 1905 by developer Abbot Kinney, who modeled the waterways on the canals of Venice, Italy, as the centerpiece of his famed 'Venice of America' seaside resort.

Six of the original canals survive today - Carroll, Linnie, Howland and Sherman Canals running east to west, crossed by Eastern Canal and Grand Canal running north to south. The lanes between them are lined with a remarkable mix of architecture, from early 20th-century bungalows and Mediterranean Revival houses to bold modern designs.

Walking the quiet pedestrian paths and arched footbridges, you can enjoy tranquil water views, abundant water birds, and a living piece of Los Angeles history. It is an ideal destination for photographers and for visitors seeking a peaceful, photogenic corner of the city.

sections.title: Historical Background
sections.content:
The story of the canal district begins in 1905, when developer Abbot Kinney unveiled 'Venice of America' - a seaside resort built to evoke the Italian city of Venice. Crews dug a network of saltwater canals across former marshland, and gondolas ferried visitors between attractions along the waterways.

By the 1920s the automobile boom made the slow canals seem outdated. After Kinney's death in 1920 the resort declined, and in 1929 Los Angeles filled in most of the waterways to create paved streets. Of the original network, only six canals were spared.

Recognition of the survivors grew gradually: the district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982 and designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 270 in 1983. After years of deterioration, the canals, walkways and bridges were fully restored in the early 1990s and reopened in 1993, launching the neighborhood's revival as one of Los Angeles' most loved and most photographed places.

sections.title: District Features
sections.content:
Six canals survive from the original 1905 network:

• Carroll, Linnie, Howland and Sherman Canals run east to west across the district
• Eastern Canal and Grand Canal run north to south along the edges

Between the waterways, quiet pedestrian lanes are lined with a rich mix of housing - early bungalows, Mediterranean Revival homes and striking contemporary architecture. Private arched bridges and footpaths cross every canal, creating the intimate, water-fronted streetscape that draws visitors from around the world.

sections.title: Location
sections.content:
The surviving canal district sits in the Venice area of Los Angeles, roughly between Washington Boulevard to the north and Venice Boulevard to the south, with Pacific Avenue to the east and Strongs Drive to the west. The official address is Venice, CA 90292.

Downtown Los Angeles is about a 30-40 minute drive away, and the district is a short walk from the sand at Venice Beach. Street parking nearby is limited and time-restricted, so many visitors park in public lots around Venice Boulevard and walk in, or arrive by bike along the beachfront bike path.

sections.title: Ecological Environment
sections.content:
The canal district is not only a historic neighborhood but also a small tidal ecosystem. Because the canals are flushed with seawater, visitors regularly spot:

• Water birds such as ducks, egrets, herons and cormorants
• Fish moving with the tide through the channels
• Canal-side gardens with native and subtropical plants
• Sea lions and seals visiting from the nearby marina and ocean

Please respect residents' privacy, keep voices low, stay on public walkways, and help preserve this remarkable historic ecosystem.

sections.title: The Dream of 'Venice of America'
sections.content:
Before Abbot Kinney built his canals, Venice Beach was little more than coastal marshland. Kinney, who had made his fortune in the tobacco business, dreamed of a cultural seaside resort to rival the great cities of Europe - an 'American Venice' with canals instead of streets.

When the resort opened in July 1905, visitors found a fantasy landscape: gondolas gliding through the waterways, an arcaded business district inspired by Venetian architecture, and a long pleasure pier jutting into the Pacific. At its peak, the original waterway grid covered an area several times larger than today's district, with more than a dozen named canals threading between the streets.

sections.title: The Great Fill of 1929
sections.content:
After Kinney's death in 1920, 'Venice of America' began to unravel. The canals were costly to maintain, motorists complained about the low bridges, and public opinion turned against the watery streets.

In 1929, Los Angeles officials voted to fill in most of the waterways, converting them into ordinary paved roads. The streets that replaced the canals still trace their original courses today - Lion Canal became Windward Avenue, Coral Canal became Main Street, and Venus Canal became San Juan Avenue. Residents who had grown up beside the water watched their canals disappear, but a handful survived.

By the 1960s and 1970s even these six survivors had fallen into decay. Crumbling seawalls and murky water led some officials to propose filling them too - a threat that galvanized local residents, including the Venice Canals Association, into decades of advocacy to save the neighborhood.

sections.title: Preservation and Revival
sections.content:
The turning point came in 1982, when the six remaining canals were listed on the National Register of Historic Places; the following year the City of Los Angeles named the district Historic-Cultural Monument No. 270. Yet official recognition alone could not fix aging infrastructure.

Through the late 1980s and early 1990s, city engineers, preservation specialists and residents joined forces on a complete restoration: new seawalls, rebuilt walkways and pedestrian bridges, and a cleaner system for circulating seawater through the canals. When the refurbished waterways reopened in 1993, the neighborhood was transformed. Property values climbed rapidly, and the canal district - once a neglected leftover of a failed dream - became one of Los Angeles' most desirable and most photographed addresses.

sections.title: Artists, Film and Everyday Life
sections.content:
Venice has attracted artists, writers and free spirits since the early 1900s, and that creative character still shapes the area around the canals. The arched bridges and mirror-still water of the district have drawn film crews and photographers for decades, providing backdrops for countless films, television shows, music videos and magazine shoots.

Through it all, the canal district remains first and foremost a real, working residential neighborhood. Kayakers and paddleboarders pass along the nearby marina channels, joggers and cyclists use the beachfront path, and residents tend gardens where ducks and herons come to visit.

Visitors are welcome on the public walkways and bridges, and the neighborhood simply asks everyone to be quiet, courteous and respectful of the private homes that line the water.

transport.fromStationDesc: Take the Metro E Line from Union Station directly to Downtown Santa Monica, then transfer to a local bus or rideshare to Venice Canals.

transport.publicTransportDesc: Take LA Metro Expo Line to Downtown Santa Monica station, then transfer to bus or bike share to reach the canal district.
transport.walkingDesc: If you're staying at a hotel near Venice Beach, you can walk or bike to the canal district.
transport.drivingDesc: There is street parking around the canal district, but pay attention to parking restrictions and time limits. It is recommended to park near Venice Blvd.

route.title: Recommended Visit Route
route.overview: Venice Canal Historic District is perfect for a 1-2 hour leisurely visit. We recommend arriving in the morning or evening, strolling along the pedestrian walkways beside the canals, and enjoying the beautiful architecture and tranquil water views. Plan about 1-2 hours for the entire visit.
steps: Start at the district entrance on Venice Boulevard where Dell Avenue meets it, then step onto the first canal footpath
Follow the path along Carroll Canal, one of the four east-west canals, and enjoy the calm water views
Cross the arched pedestrian bridges and photograph the reflections from different angles
Continue along Linnie, Howland and Sherman Canals to see how each waterway has its own character
Walk down Grand Canal or Eastern Canal, the two north-south waterways that frame the district
Rest on a bench beside the water and take in the quiet neighbourhood atmosphere
Finish by walking the short distance to Venice Beach (about 10 minutes) to continue your day

amenities.title: Visitor Facilities & Practical Information
amenities.subtitle: A neutral, type-level overview of public facilities around the Venice canal district, so you can plan a comfortable visit - no individual businesses are endorsed.

items.title: Public Restrooms
items.desc: Restrooms are not located along the residential canal lanes. The nearest public restrooms are the beachfront facilities along the oceanfront walk and the public plaza near the beach end of Windward Avenue.
items.tip: Make a restroom stop before entering the canal lanes.

items.title: Parking
items.desc: On-street parking is limited and time-restricted, and several streets in the surrounding neighbourhoods are residential permit zones. Paid public lots can be found in the beachfront area and along Venice Boulevard.
items.tip: Read every sign twice - parking rules change from block to block.

items.title: Dining Options
items.desc: The canal lanes themselves are residential and have no food service. Casual cafes, coffee shops, healthy eateries and takeout stands line the oceanfront walk and Abbot Kinney Boulevard a short walk away.
items.tip: Carry a water bottle; public drinking fountains are found mainly along the beachfront.

items.title: Grocery & Convenience Stores
items.desc: Neighbourhood markets, small specialty grocers and convenience stores serve the Venice area along main corridors such as Lincoln Boulevard and Washington Boulevard, a short drive or longer walk from the district.
items.tip: Stock up on water and snacks before your visit to stay self-sufficient.

items.title: Places to Stay (by Type)
items.desc: Within easy reach you will find beachfront hotels, smaller boutique guesthouses and vacation rentals in surrounding residential streets, plus a wider range of hotels in nearby Santa Monica and Marina del Rey.
items.tip: Accommodation near the coast is popular in summer - book well in advance.

items.title: Fuel & EV Charging
items.desc: Fuel stations are located on the main arterials around Venice, such as Lincoln Boulevard and Centinela Avenue and near Marina del Rey. Public electric-vehicle charging is available at many paid parking lots and shopping areas in the region.
items.tip: EV drivers should check charger availability in advance, as demand is high on weekends.

items.title: Pharmacy & Medical Help
items.desc: Pharmacies and urgent-care clinics can be found along the commercial corridors around the district, and full hospital services are a short drive away in Santa Monica.
items.tip: Save the address of the nearest urgent-care clinic before your trip.

items.title: Accessibility
items.desc: The canal walkways are pedestrian paths with steps and arched pedestrian bridges, so access for wheelchairs and strollers is limited in places. Flat sidewalk-level routes along adjacent streets and the beach path offer easier alternatives.
items.tip: Ask your accommodation for the most accessible route before setting out.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Venice Canal Historic District
faq.intro: Quick answers to the questions visitors ask most about the Venice canals.

items.q: Where is Venice Canal Historic District located?
items.a: Venice Canal Historic District is located in the Venice neighborhood of Los Angeles, California, United States (Venice, CA 90292).

items.q: Is Venice Canal Historic District free to visit?
items.a: Yes, Venice Canal Historic District is a public neighborhood that is free to visit year-round and is open 24 hours a day.

items.q: How far are the Venice Canals from Venice Beach?
items.a: The canal district sits just inland from the shore - about a 5-10 minute walk east of the Venice Beach Boardwalk and Ocean Front Walk.

items.q: Can you rent boats or kayaks in the Venice canals?
items.a: There are no boat- or kayak-rental stands inside the canal district - it is a residential tidal waterway, not a rental venue. Visitors are welcome to paddle human-powered craft (kayaks, canoes and rowboats) that they bring themselves, provided they are non-motorized and follow local rules. Motorboats are not allowed. The nearest kayak and stand-up-paddleboard rentals are at the Venice Beach oceanfront and the nearby marina.

items.q: When was Venice Canal Historic District built?
items.a: The canals were built in 1905 by developer Abbot Kinney, who modeled the waterways on the canal system of Venice, Italy.

items.q: How many canals are there in Venice Canal Historic District?
items.a: Six historic canals survive from the original network: Carroll, Linnie, Howland and Sherman Canals run east to west, crossed by Eastern Canal and Grand Canal running north to south.

items.q: What is the best time to visit the Venice canals?
items.a: Early morning and late afternoon offer the softest light and fewest crowds, and weekdays are noticeably quieter than weekends.

items.q: Can you swim or boat in the Venice canals?
items.a: Swimming is not allowed in the canals. Non-motorized, human-powered boating (kayaks, canoes, rowboats) is permitted for visitors who bring their own compliant craft and use the designated public access points - motorboats are prohibited. Keep noise low, stay clear of private docks and respect the residential neighborhood. Always check current local regulations before you go.

items.q: Where can I park near Venice Canal Historic District?
items.a: Street parking around the district is limited and time-restricted. Parking near Venice Boulevard or at nearby public lots and walking in is recommended.

items.q: Is Venice Canal Historic District worth visiting?
items.a: Yes - listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982 and beautifully restored in the 1990s, it is one of Los Angeles' most picturesque and photogenic places.

officialManagement.title: About Venice Canal Historic District
officialManagement.text:
Venice Canal Historic District is a historic canal neighborhood in the Venice area of Los Angeles, California, created in 1905 by developer Abbot Kinney as the centerpiece of his 'Venice of America' resort.

Six of the original canals survive today, lined with residential architecture of many styles. The district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982 and fully restored in the early 1990s. Whether you are strolling the quiet walkways beside the water or admiring the architecture, this neighborhood offers a uniquely Los Angeles experience.

walking-map.metaTitle: Venice Canals Walking Map & Loop | Free Self-Guided Route
walking-map.metaDescription: A practical Venice Canals walking map: the full loop distance, time, entrances, arched bridges and the best order to explore the historic district on foot.
walking-map.h1: Venice Canals Walking Map & Self-Guided Loop
walking-map.intro: The Venice Canal Historic District is best explored on foot. The six surviving canals form a compact, walkable grid of quiet pedestrian paths and arched footbridges. This walking map gives you a simple loop, realistic timing and the key access points so you can see the whole district in under an hour.

sections.title: The Loop at a Glance
sections.content: A relaxed circuit of all six canals covers roughly 1 mile (1.6 km) and takes about 45-60 minutes, including photo stops. The route is flat and entirely on public walkways - no streets to cross except at the entrance. Start and finish at the same point so you never backtrack.

sections.title: Where to Start
sections.content: Most visitors begin where Dell Avenue meets Venice Boulevard, just west of Pacific Avenue. This is the main gateway to the canal district and the easiest place to park or arrive on foot from Venice Beach (about a 10-minute walk east). A small bridge here drops you straight onto the first canal path.

sections.title: Suggested Walking Order
sections.content: 1) Cross the entry bridge onto Carroll Canal and walk its length east to west. 2) Turn onto the Grand Canal or Eastern Canal along the district edge. 3) Loop back via Linnie, Howland and Sherman Canals, each with its own character. 4) Recross the arched footbridges for reflections and different angles. 5) Return to the Venice Boulevard gateway. Signage is minimal, so follow the water - every path eventually leads back to a perimeter street.

sections.title: Bridges & Crossings
sections.content: The private arched footbridges are the district's signature photo opportunity. They cross every canal and connect the residential lanes. Stay on the public bridges and paths; the residences and docks between them are private. The perimeter streets (Venice Blvd to the south, Washington Blvd to the north) are where you rejoin the sidewalk grid.

sections.title: Accessibility
sections.content: The canal paths are pedestrian walkways with steps and arched bridges in places, so wheelchair and stroller access is limited. Flatter alternatives run along the adjacent perimeter streets and the nearby beach path. If mobility is a concern, plan a shorter out-and-back along the Grand Canal rather than the full loop.

faq.q: How long does the Venice Canals walking loop take?
faq.a: A full loop of all six canals takes about 45-60 minutes at a relaxed pace with photo stops. A shorter out-and-back along the Grand Canal can be done in 20-30 minutes.

faq.q: Where do I start the Venice Canals walk?
faq.a: Start where Dell Avenue meets Venice Boulevard, just west of Pacific Avenue. It is the main gateway, the easiest place to park, and about a 10-minute walk from Venice Beach.

faq.q: Is the Venice Canals walk free?
faq.a: Yes. The canals are a public residential neighborhood with free, open walkways. There is no ticket, tour fee or reservation required to walk the paths.

faq.q: Can I bring a stroller or wheelchair on the canal paths?
faq.a: Access is limited because some paths have steps and arched bridges. Flat perimeter streets and the beach path offer easier alternatives. A shorter Grand Canal out-and-back is the most manageable option.

parking-directions.metaTitle: Venice Canals Parking & Directions | Where to Park
parking-directions.metaDescription: Where to park for the Venice Canals: street rules, public lots near Venice Boulevard, driving directions from Downtown LA and LAX, and transit or bike options.
parking-directions.h1: Parking & Directions for the Venice Canals
parking-directions.intro: Parking near the Venice Canal Historic District is limited and time-restricted, so a little planning goes a long way. This guide covers the street rules, the most reliable public lots, and the easiest ways to get there by car, transit or bike.

sections.title: Street Parking Rules
sections.content: On-street parking around the canals is scarce and many surrounding blocks are residential permit zones where curb markings restrict non-resident parking, often for only 1-2 hours. Always read every sign twice - rules change from block to block. The safest street options are along Venice Boulevard and the perimeter streets, a short walk from the water.

sections.title: Public Parking Lots
sections.content: Paid public lots are concentrated along the Venice Boulevard corridor and the beachfront area near Windward Avenue. The beachfront lots are the largest and most reliable, especially on weekends; from there it is a pleasant 10-15 minute walk to the canal gateway. Arrive before late morning on weekends to avoid full lots.

sections.title: Where to Park
sections.content: Best balance: a beachfront lot near Windward Avenue, then walk east to the canals. Closest to the water: metered street spots on Venice Boulevard near Dell Avenue (time-limited). Avoid circling the narrow residential canal streets - there is no through-traffic parking and it disturbs residents.

sections.title: Driving Directions
sections.content: From Downtown LA: I-10 W to I-405 S, exit Venice Boulevard and head west to the coast. From LAX: take Lincoln Boulevard north to Venice Boulevard, then west. Both are roughly 20-40 minutes depending on traffic. Use a navigation app and set the destination to 'Venice Boulevard & Pacific Avenue' rather than the canals themselves, since the residential streets are not drivable through.

sections.title: By Transit & Bike
sections.content: The Metro E (Expo) Line reaches Downtown Santa Monica, where you can transfer to a local bus or ride-share the final miles. The Venice Beach bike path connects the canals to Santa Monica and Marina del Rey, making cycling one of the most pleasant, traffic-free ways to arrive.

faq.q: Is parking free at the Venice Canals?
faq.a: Street parking is free where allowed but heavily time-restricted and mostly permit-only near the canals. Public lots are paid. There is no free dedicated canal parking lot.

faq.q: Where is the closest parking to the Venice Canals?
faq.a: Metered street spaces on Venice Boulevard near Dell Avenue are closest, but limited. The most reliable nearby parking is the beachfront lots near Windward Avenue, about a 10-15 minute walk away.

faq.q: Can I park on the canal streets themselves?
faq.a: Most canal-side streets are residential permit zones with strict limits, and the lanes are not through-traffic. It is better to park on Venice Boulevard or a beachfront lot and walk in.

faq.q: How far is parking from the canals?
faq.a: From the beachfront lots it is about a 10-15 minute walk. From Venice Boulevard street parking it is a 2-5 minute walk to the gateway at Dell Avenue.

visitor-guide.h1: Venice Canal Historic District Visitor Guide
visitor-guide.intro: The Venice Canal Historic District is a free, always-open residential neighborhood built around six historic canals. This visitor guide covers everything you need before you go: entry, timing, what to bring, the rules that keep the district peaceful, and the facilities nearby.

sections.title: Entry, Tickets & Reservations
sections.content: There are no tickets, no entry fee and no reservation required. The canals are a public neighborhood open 24 hours a day, year-round. You simply walk in via the pedestrian paths and arched bridges. Guided tours are occasionally offered by local historical societies but are not needed to enjoy the district.

sections.title: Best Time to Visit
sections.content: Early morning (7-9 AM) and late afternoon to evening offer the softest light and the fewest crowds - ideal for photography and a peaceful stroll. Weekdays are noticeably quieter than weekends. Mornings in any season are calm; summer evenings avoid the midday heat.

sections.title: What to Bring
sections.content: Bring a camera or phone (the district is very photogenic), water, and a light layer for ocean breezes. Comfortable shoes are all you need for the flat paths. There are no shops or food stands inside the canal lanes, so pick up snacks and drinks beforehand.

sections.title: Rules & Etiquette
sections.content: The canals are a living residential community. Keep voices low, stay on the public walkways and bridges, and do not enter private docks or gardens. Swimming is not allowed. Non-motorized, human-powered boating (kayaks, canoes, rowboats) is permitted for visitors who bring their own compliant craft from designated public access points; motorboats are prohibited. Always check current local regulations before boating.

sections.title: Facilities Nearby
sections.content: There are no public restrooms inside the canal lanes - use the beachfront facilities along the oceanfront walk before you enter. Cafes, restaurants and shops line the nearby oceanfront and Abbot Kinney Boulevard. The nearest urgent-care and pharmacies are a short drive away along the commercial corridors.

faq.q: Do I need tickets for the Venice Canal Historic District?
faq.a: No. Entry is free and open to the public 24/7. There are no tickets, no reservation and no gate. You simply walk the public paths.

faq.q: Are dogs allowed at the Venice Canals?
faq.a: Leashed dogs are generally allowed on the public walkways, but be respectful of residents and clean up after your pet. Some paths are narrow, so keep dogs close.

faq.q: Are there restrooms at the Venice Canals?
faq.a: No public restrooms are inside the canal lanes. The nearest facilities are along the Venice Beach oceanfront walk, a short walk away - plan to use them before entering.

faq.q: How much time should I budget for the Venice Canals?
faq.a: A relaxed walk of all six canals takes about 45-60 minutes. If you just want a quick look, 20-30 minutes along the Grand Canal is enough.

photo-spots.metaTitle: Best Venice Canals Photo Spots & Golden Hour Tips
photo-spots.metaDescription: The best Venice Canals photo spots: arched bridges, Grand Canal reflections, walkways and sunsets, plus golden-hour timing and drone rules.
photo-spots.h1: Best Photo Spots at the Venice Canals
photo-spots.intro: The Venice Canal Historic District is one of Los Angeles' most photogenic corners. Mirror-still water, arched footbridges and Mediterranean-style homes make it a favorite for photographers. Here are the top spots and the timing that makes them shine.

sections.title: Best Light & Timing
sections.content: Golden hour - roughly the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset - gives soft, warm light and the calmest water for reflections. Early morning also means fewer people and undisturbed reflections. Overcast days still work well, with even, diffuse light that flatters the architecture.

sections.title: Top Photo Spots
sections.content: 1) The arched footbridges - shoot down the canal with the bridge framing the water and houses. 2) Grand Canal waterfront - wide, tranquil views and elegant residences. 3) The pedestrian walkway - intimate, everyday-life scenes along the water. 4) Mediterranean Revival architecture - detail shots of the historic homes. 5) Sunset on the water - golden reflections from any bridge facing west.

sections.title: Photography Tips
sections.content: Get low at bridge level for stronger reflections. Use a polarizing filter to cut glare on the water. A standard or wide lens is enough; a tripod helps at blue hour but mind the narrow paths. Be patient and wait for foot-traffic gaps for clean compositions.

faq.q: What is the best time to photograph the Venice Canals?
faq.a: Early morning and the hour before sunset (golden hour) offer the best light and calmest water for reflections, plus fewer people. Arrive at sunrise for undisturbed mirror reflections.

faq.q: Where is the best sunset spot at the Venice Canals?
faq.a: Any arched footbridge facing west captures golden-hour reflections on the water. The Grand Canal waterfront also frames warm sunset light on the residences.

faq.q: Can I fly a drone over the Venice Canals?
faq.a: The canals are within controlled airspace near the coast and over a residential area, and the U.S. has strict drone rules. Recreational drone flight is generally not appropriate here - check FAA rules and local ordinances before flying, and respect residents' privacy.

faq.q: Are tripods allowed on the canal paths?
faq.a: Yes, but the paths are narrow and shared with pedestrians and residents. Use a compact travel tripod and step aside so you do not block the walkway.

history.metaTitle: History of the Venice Canals | Abbot Kinney & Venice of America
history.metaDescription: The story of the Venice Canals: Abbot Kinney's 1905 Venice of America, the 1929 fill, and the 1982-1993 preservation that saved six canals.
history.intro: The Venice Canals are the surviving remnant of a fantastical 1905 seaside resort called 'Venice of America.' Their story spans ambition, decline, a controversial 1929 fill, and a hard-won preservation that turned a faded neighborhood into one of Los Angeles' most beloved landmarks.

sections.title: Abbot Kinney & 1905
sections.content: Developer Abbot Kinney - who made his fortune in tobacco - dreamed of an American Venice. In 1905 he opened 'Venice of America' on former marshland, with a network of saltwater canals modeled on Venice, Italy, gondolas ferrying tourists, an arcaded business district and a long pleasure pier. At its peak the grid covered far more ground than today's district.

sections.title: The Venice of America Era
sections.content: For a few glamorous years the canals were the centerpiece of a thriving resort. But the automobile boom of the 1920s made the slow waterways feel outdated, and public opinion turned against them. After Kinney's death in 1920 the resort declined.

sections.title: The Great Fill of 1929
sections.content: In 1929 Los Angeles voted to fill most of the canals and convert them into paved streets. Many of those streets still trace the old waterways - Lion Canal became Windward Avenue, Coral Canal became Main Street, Venus Canal became San Juan Avenue. Only six canals survived.

sections.title: Preservation & Revival
sections.content: The six surviving canals were listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982 and named Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 270 in 1983. After decades of decay, a full restoration of the seawalls, walkways and bridges was completed and the canals reopened in 1993, sparking the neighborhood's revival.

sections.title: The Canals Today
sections.content: Six canals remain: Carroll, Linnie, Howland and Sherman run east-west, crossed by Eastern Canal and Grand Canal running north-south. They are lined with a remarkable mix of early bungalows, Mediterranean Revival homes and bold modern architecture - a living piece of Los Angeles history.

faq.q: Who built the Venice Canals?
faq.a: The canals were built in 1905 by developer Abbot Kinney as the centerpiece of his 'Venice of America' resort, modeled on the canals of Venice, Italy.

faq.q: When were the Venice Canals built and restored?
faq.a: They were built in 1905 and largely filled in 1929, leaving six. Those six were listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982 and fully restored, reopening in 1993.

faq.q: Why were most of the canals filled in?
faq.a: By the late 1920s the canals were costly to maintain and unpopular with motorists; in 1929 the city voted to fill most of them and turn them into streets. Only six were spared.

faq.q: How many Venice Canals are there today?
faq.a: Six historic canals survive: Carroll, Linnie, Howland and Sherman (east-west), crossed by Eastern Canal and Grand Canal (north-south).
